source.title: Revisiting the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis
source.authors: Mohit Raghavendra; Vaskar Nath; Sean M. Hendryx

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a power-law relationship extends to supervised post-training, measuring benchmark task accuracy as the number of fine-tuning examples increases; it also compares performance across model sizes.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the post-training task-accuracy scaling curves and their fitted coefficients. The paper also reports that higher-quality instruction data scales better, but does not give numerical values or fit coefficients for that comparison. Results on win rates, error categories, and new-knowledge integration do not test the listed scaling versions and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of benchmark accuracy against the number of supervised fine-tuning examples (100 to 10k) for Llama-2, Llama-3 and Mistral (Tables 7–8, Figs 1–2). This is a new regime for V5. The size comparison at 7B to 70B bears on V6. The measure is task accuracy rather than loss, the fits span only about two orders of magnitude, and no goodness of fit is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. SFT task accuracy follows a power law in fine-tuning examples across families and sizes, more consistently on reasoning tasks. The central aim is to argue that the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis is an over-simplification. Further points: gains are driven by reasoning rather than formatting, win rates mislead, and reasoning post-training helps integrate new knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: Measures benchmark task accuracy after supervised fine-tuning against example count and selected model sizes, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameters, tokens, or compute. The paper does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report more consistent and predictable data scaling on reasoning-centric tasks than on subjective instruction-following tasks. They also state that performance scales better with higher-quality instruction data; no numerical fit comparison is given for that ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning scaling curves depend on data quality: ConiferHard scales better than ConiferEasy and Dolly (Fig. 7, qualitative). Larger models' curves bend upward rather than shifting in parallel.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning data-scaling exponents depend on dataset quality and base-model size.

record.problems: The reported scaling results are for supervised post-training benchmark accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss. The main accuracy curves are presented in figures, while the text provides fitted coefficients but not fit uncertainty or uncertainty intervals. Only selected model families, tasks, and sizes are evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. The instruction-data-quality comparison in Figure 7 is not separately rowed because the text gives only a qualitative statement and no numerical outcome or fitted coefficients.

untested.parts: Other modalities, repeated data, transfer, RLHF; loss rather than accuracy; ranges beyond about 10k examples.
Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted law in model size (only 2–3 sizes per family, ordering only).

missing.what: GSM1k contamination check showing a similar accuracy scaling trend for Llama-3-8b GSM8k-trained models.

record.verdict_notes: The power law is in accuracy, not loss, and the fits cannot include the D=0 point. Coefficients are given without uncertainty. Whether an accuracy power law counts as 'the same power-law form' for V5 is a judgement call. V6 evidence is qualitative ordering across 2–3 sizes.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not fit laws on small pretraining runs and test predictions on much larger runs.
Does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation for fixed compute or measure its scaling with compute.
Does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests supervised text fine-tuning by number of examples and benchmark task accuracy. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, transfer, or held-out pretraining loss.

Tests benchmark task accuracy across selected model sizes and post-training example counts. Does not test predictability from pretraining loss or downstream performance across other tasks and settings.

Does not test whether published pretraining exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with parameter counting, training schedule, or fitting method, or whether pretraining loss curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: SFT on reasoning tasks (GSM8k, SubQA, coding), sub-10B and 13–70B models
relationships.reason: Accuracy fits P=aD^(1/b) for all models and tasks, per text and Tables 7–8 (r01–r09, r16–r19, r22–r27).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fitted P=aD^(1/b) across all tested models and reasoning tasks.

relationships.condition: Instruction following (Conifer, Dolly) and the form of the law
relationships.reason: Authors call IF scaling less consistent and predictable (r10–r15, r20, r21, r28–r30). The law is in accuracy, not loss, over about two decades with no fit error reported.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy scaling was less consistent and predictable over about two decades, with no fit error reported.

relationships.condition: Llama-2 7/13/70B and Llama-3 8/70B on Math, SubQA, Conifer
relationships.reason: Text says larger models consistently outperform smaller at equal data; ordering only, no size law (r16–r30).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models consistently outperform smaller models given equal data, although no quantitative size law is established.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
